one_liner: Header-only SIMD open-addressing hash map/set for Boost; unordered_flat_map is 2.7x-11.6x faster than std::unordered_map.
what_it_does: Boost.Unordered is a family of hash containers: std-conformant closed-addressing boost::unordered_map/set, open-addressing boost::unordered_flat_map/set and pointer-stable boost::unordered_node_map/set, plus boost::concurrent_flat_map/set for multithreaded use. unordered_flat_map does the same job as std::unordered_map but stores elements directly in a SIMD-probed bucket array instead of per-bucket linked lists. API tracks std::unordered_map closely (heterogeneous lookup, try_emplace, contains) but diverges where the layout forces it: no node extraction, erase(iterator) returns a proxy object, begin() is not O(1).
how_it_is_fast: Elements sit in groups of 15 slots backed by a 16-byte metadata word (per-slot reduced hash byte plus an overflow byte); SSE2/Neon SIMD scans the whole metadata word in one op to rule out non-matching slots before touching real elements, with quadratic probing to the next group on overflow (non-SIMD architectures emulate this via bit-interleaving). The library also auto-post-mixes ('avalanches') whatever hash function you supply so a poor-quality hash doesn't degrade open-addressing performance, at a small cost you can opt out of by declaring your hash `is_avalanching`.
when_to_use: uint64_t or other cheap-to-hash keys, 1-2M+ entries, throughput-bound build/find/churn/iterate workloads
Whole-container iteration is common — flat layout iterates 11.6x faster than std::unordered_map on u64 keys
x86-64 (SSE2) or aarch64 (Neon) targets that benefit from SIMD metadata scanning
Want boost::unordered_map's near-drop-in API but don't need pointer/reference stability across mutation
Already use Boost, or can add a header-only dependency with no link step
when_not_to_use: Code relies on pointer/reference stability across insert/erase — use boost::unordered_node_map or std::unordered_map
Memory is tighter than speed: in the same benchmark std::unordered_map had lower peak RSS per u64 entry (45.78 B) than every flat map
Can't tolerate Boost's transitive include weight — issue #195 flags a large transitive-include graph hurting compile times
Need concurrent mutation from multiple threads — use boost::concurrent_flat_map instead, unordered_flat_map has no built-in synchronization
Bulk-loading one flat_map from another already-hashed container via a plain insert loop without reserve() first — open issue #178 documents quadratic insertion in that pattern

integration.dependencies: Boost (Boost.Container_hash, Boost.Core, Boost.Config, Boost.Assert and other Boost headers pulled in transitively)
integration.platforms: any; SIMD-accelerated on x86-64 (SSE2) and aarch64 (Neon), portable bit-interleaved metadata scan elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: not documented for unordered_flat_map itself (ordinary container assumption: concurrent reads only); use boost::concurrent_flat_map/node_map for concurrent mutation
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: std::unordered_map API surface mostly matches, but no pointer/reference stability across insert/erase, begin() is not O(1), erase(iterator) returns a proxy not an iterator, no bucket iteration API, and max_load_factor isn't user-settable

gotchas: Inserting into a flat_map by iterating another (already hash-ordered) container with plain insert() can degrade to quadratic time; call reserve() first or use the copy constructor instead (open issue boostorg/unordered#178)
Open addressing is hash-quality sensitive; the library auto post-mixes your hash unless it's tagged `using is_avalanching = std::true_type;`, which skips the safety net for a small speed gain
erase(iterator) returns a proxy object convertible to an iterator, not an iterator directly — code that assumes the std return type may need adjustment
value_type must be move-constructible and there's no pointer stability under rehash or node extraction/insertion API (use boost::unordered_node_map if you need those)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Boost.Unordered when you want one vendor for the whole hash-container family (flat/node/concurrent variants, all header-only) rather than a single map type; abseil's absl::flat_hash_map is faster on these exact numbers (5.99x vs 5.00x build+destroy, 2.43x vs 2.70x find) but pulls in more of the Abseil ecosystem, and ankerl::unordered_dense is a smaller single-header option that wins on pure iteration speed but has no concurrent or pointer-stable variants.
verified_claims_summary: On unordered_dense's public bench_readme.sh harness (clang 22.1.8, -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++20, transparent huge pages, one pinned core, Fedora 44, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X), boost::unordered_flat_map was 5.00x faster build+destroy, 2.70x faster find, 4.66x faster churn, and 11.60x faster iterate than std::unordered_map (libstdc++, inferred) on uint64_t keys, with 1.55x-32.9x gains on std::string keys.
status_note: Actively maintained core Boost module (last commit 2026-06-17); BSL-1.0 licensed and header-only, so it's trivially vendorable despite the standalone module mirror's low star count — it ships inside every Boost install and is used far more broadly than that number suggests.
